props.title: Carefree
props.initialSlug: Rogers dances into psychiatrist's heart & mind

sections.content: Carefree represents a pivotal moment in Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers' legendary partnership, marking their first explicit romantic comedy where dance takes a relative backseat to plot. The film's screwball elements and psychological comedy premise - with Astaire playing a psychiatrist trying to analyze Rogers' romantic troubles - showcases RKO's attempt to freshen their winning formula. This shift followed their massive success with Swing Time (1936) and Shall We Dance (1937), as audiences began craving more substantial plots alongside the dancing.

sections.content: The film's standout sequence, "The Yam," demonstrates a fascinating evolution in their dance style. Unlike the elegant ballroom numbers of Top Hat (1935), this routine incorporates playful athletic moves and even a golf course setting. Director Mark Sandrich, who helmed five Astaire-Rogers vehicles, brings a lighter touch here, allowing their natural chemistry to shine through the comedic situations rather than relying solely on their dancing prowess.

The psychological elements in Carefree actually prefigured later films like Lady in the Dark (1944) and Spellbound (1945) in bringing psychoanalysis to mainstream Hollywood. Irving Berlin's score, while not his most memorable, includes the clever "Change Partners," which earned an Academy Award nomination and became a jazz standard covered by artists from Billie Holiday to Tony Bennett. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Movie Musicals

movies.title: Roberta
movies.slug: Luxurious fashion-world setting showcases their sophisticated style alongside Irene Dunne

sections.content: Carefree arrived at a crucial turning point for Hollywood musicals. The elaborate Busby Berkeley spectacles like Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933) were giving way to more plot-driven entertainments. This shift would ultimately lead to the integrated musicals of the 1940s and 1950s, where songs advanced the plot rather than merely interrupting it, as perfected in films like On the Town (1949) and Singin' in the Rain (1952).
